div.p: This paper describes a software architecture for parallel kinematic machines and its evolvement to a self-adaptive system striving to optimize, protect and heal itself. Self-* properties are provided by selfmanager components that observe and manipulate their associated system parts. A development approach for the self-managers is outlined, as is a first realization of a self-manager responsible for the control core. This self-manager distributes control components during runtime and makes feasibility decisions based on a runtime schedulability analysis.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Complexity and its handling has become a major issue over the last few years. The increasing size and connectivity of distributed and possibly heterogeneous systems has led to difficulties in maintainability and extendibility. Intricate errors in technical systems leading to unpredictable and in cases catastrophic behavior are still a common sight, even though huge quality assurance efforts are undertaken.

Several proposals have been made to handle the ever increasing system complexity and the according problems. Most of them have in common that they try to handle the complexity with nature inspired concepts. IBM suggested an autonomic approach in the year 2001, later refined in [1], and Organic Computing has established as new research field [2]. By creating technical systems consisting of multitudes of selfmanaged components that adapt their behavior according to environmental changes and aim specifications it is possible to achieve such advantageous properties as self-healing, selfoptimization, self-protection or self-configuration also summarized as self-* properties [3]. As a result one does not only gain control of the complexity but can create very robust and fault-tolerant systems that can adapt to changing conditions or even protect themselves from environmental hazards.
Such Autonomic Computing systems derive their macroscopic behavior from local observation and communication of their agent-like subsystems.

Due to this and the ever possible changing of component aims or behavior, it is very difficult to formally verify properties for autonomic computing systems. Some model-based approaches use assume/guarantee or compositional verification [4], some use simulation techniques [5].

It still is unclear what kind of engineering approach is the best for autonomic or organic systems even if advances have been made in that region that transfer some of the classic system engineering approaches to this new domain [6,7,8].

This paper introduces self-management components in a software architecture for robotic control that allow the realization of self-* properties for its components. It further shows how functional and real-time correctness can be ensured by the application of formal and lightweight formal methods during the design and later during the runtime of the system.

In Section 2, our software architecture, its components and its real-time layers are described. Section 3 focuses on the creation, validation and integration of the management components. A selfoptimization approach ensuring the adherence of functional and real-time properties with a runtime schedulability analysis is presented as a case study in Section 4. Section 5 concludes.

div.head: Software architecture
div.p: The software architecture PROSA-X (Parallel RObots Software Architecture -eXtended) [9], developed in our interdisciplinary research project, has been designed for the control of Parallel Kinematic Machines (PKMs). With their closed kinematic chains and low moved masses, those robots come with beneficial attributes like high structural stiffness, outstanding precision and a high payload to robot mass ratio [10]. PKMs are able to move very fast. The high accelerations and velocities require high control cycle frequencies and thus induced several hard real-time constraints for our software architecture. The real-time capabilities were one of the cornerstones of our architecture, another one was generality. As a result PROSA-X is capable to control totally different robots without the need to swap behavioral parts.

The whole engineering process was interwoven with an extensive model-driven approach that allowed several different quality assurance measures [11]. 1. At the moment we are integrating image processing to enhance the fault-tolerant execution of robot tasks and better algorithms for the control core. Since this induces demand for more algorithmic power, while the control cycle frequency has to be retained, we decided to support further control PCs. This approach allows not only the distribution of the algorithmic load and thus even higher cycle frequencies but also paves the way for self-management capabilities to increase system performance and robustness.

One of the central components of our architecture, the control core RCA562, is now split and has parts running on every control PC. Those distributed parts control and coordinate the execution of all cyclic algorithmic load. All of this tasks, e.g. sensor preevaluation, trajectory planning, position and force control, are encapsulated in different motion and sensor modules that are promising candidates for a distributed control approach. Details about the control core in its single PC version can be found in [12].

Communication of the distributed system parts is realized by the same communication system we used for connecting sensors and actors until now. Those DSP devices used to connect e.g. drive amplifiers or force sensors communicate over a FireWire field bus. Since there was no commercial communication system available that fulfilled our rigid bandwidth and performance requirements, we developed a new one in our research project. It is based on a standard component IEEE1394 (FireWire) bus solution, an according bus protocol (IAP) and a real-time middleware (MiRPA-X). An in depth description of the communication layer can be found in [13].

On each of our control PCs, several real-time layers exist that safe-guard the validity of real-time constraints during execution. The hard real-time layer, for instance, contains a deterministic scheduler provided by the middleware, the FireWire bus protocol, and subordinate control and monitoring processes. Failure or time exceedance here leads to an emergency break and the entering of a global error state. The second layer is the soft real-time layer where non conformance to real-time limitations is noticed and can be treated by the system. Here for example, a skill primitive interpreter (RoboPret in Fig. 1), used to realize the error tolerant execution of robot tasks [14], resides. There is also a non real-time layer where demand-oriented system parts, like the TCP server, are working.

All tasks despite the ones in the hard real-time layer can be preempted by tasks with higher priority. QNX's priority inheritance mechanisms are used to avoid priority inversion problems. Hard real-time tasks are synchronized to a hardware timing signal and leave some time at the end of the cycle. That timeslot is used by the soft and non real-time tasks that usually take five of those timeslots to finish their cyclic work.

One self-* property already inherent to our system is self-configuration. Several system parts find and offer resources over the middleware. The control core acquires and activates necessary motion modules for an actual task on-the-fly. The IAP configures its distributed protocol instances according to current communication needs. Bandwidth reservation, bus time slot coordination, and adaptation of data marshalling structures all happen automatically.

The new distributed version of PROSA-X, however, enables the realization of several further self-* properties. For instance, self-optimization becomes possible, where performance oriented analysis and planning leads to the migration of control components and thus enables higher cycle frequencies. Selfprotection is easily thinkable, meaning monitoring the processor load and distributing calculation intensive parts before real-time constraints are actually violated.

The other way around, communication intensive parts can be concentrated on one PC to decrease bus load prior to a bandwidth related jitter. By rearranging system components after an error state is entered, for instance because the time slice for the soft real-time layer was too small, the system can heal itself and may return to normal operation.
The next section describes how we realize the selfmanagement capabilities for our architecture by the preparation and integration of management components.

div.head: Realization of self-management
div.p: Multitudes of parameters in several components developed by different partners in our interdisciplinary research project influence the behavior of our system. The amount of code lines containing instructions has already passed the 100.000 and experts from several groups are needed to tune the behavior of the system. By the introduction of self-managing components, we intend to greatly reduce the effort to maintain the system, to improve its behavior, and to decrease the integration effort necessary when new hardware and software parts are included.

The application of self-managers for system components is a standard approach to realize autonomic computing [1]. Providing components with the capability to observe and evaluate their own behavior as well as their environment is a powerful way to establish self-* properties and thus increase robustness, performance and flexibility of a system. Instead of having several experts tune system parameters to achieve an adaptation to new circumstances, the system realizes adaptations and optimizations itself. Therefore, the expert knowledge necessary to evaluate the behavior and environment of a component and to make decisions about behavioral changes has to be made available for the managing component. For this, we intend to establish a standardized, tool supported method in our project. In our toolbox, component designers specify resources relevant for the evaluation. This can be execution times, shared memory areas or externally visible component attributes. Pointers to that information will later be part of the self-manager's knowledge base. Afterwards, the expert specifies an evaluation function providing one or more index values revealing how the component currently performs. This evaluation can also trigger complex analysis procedures as later will be shown in Section 4. Then, a planning algorithm has to be specified that, depending on the evaluation results, manipulates the system parts in the according area of responsibility. The toolbox will be able to determine an appropriate real-time layer and priorities for the different threads of the self-manager. While things like case based reasoning or fuzzy inference can be performed in a hard real-time context, more complex tasks have to be realized in the soft or non real-time layers. Afterwards, QNX compliant source code will be generated that can be compiled and executed in our simulation environment [11], together with behavioral models of our architecture. The simulation can be controlled manually or by scenario based test cases capturing system requirements. This way, a first validation of the system's behavior with integrated selfmanagement components is achieved. The simulation approach can determine if there are racing conditions for shared resources or if functional and real-time requirements are met.

Additionally, we want some of the self-managers to base their decisions on formal analysis. If the analysis of a new situation is performed prior to an actual reaction of the self-manager, this reaction may be a bit slow. For critical system parts where optimization is not existential but a goal subordinate to safety, meaning functional and real-time correctness, we consider this feasible. Analysis can take part on a separate PC, whereas the result evaluation happens in a soft realtime layer on a control PC. An example for this approach is described in Section 4.

Depending on the amount of soft real-time available during execution, special online model checking algorithms as described in [15] can be applied to perform property verification during the runtime of the system. Therefore, we are investigating if our model base can be transformed to the necessary Kripke structures and Büchi automata. This way we want to realize runtime bounded model checking for our system.

There is research going on in the field of compositional verification of self-optimizing mechatronic systems by using assume guarantee techniques [4]. Such offline verification prior to an execution is at the moment not in our focus.

div.head: Runtime optimization
div.p: This section presents our first realization of a selfmanager for the control core. Its purpose is to analyze, plan and execute the distribution of control components, especially the motion and sensor modules mentioned in Section 2. After connecting additional control PCs, the system adapts to the new situation by seamlessly integrating the new hardware and migrating software parts to it. This way the system can increase its failure tolerance by e.g. redundancy or enhance its performance by rearranging its real-time layers and achieving higher cycle frequencies. We wanted the distribution of system components and adaptation to topology changes to be fully automatic. A self-manager capable to realize that (see Fig. 2) has to consider many parameters, e.g. execution times, bandwidth, or topology, and has to decide which components to migrate and most of all if the system is able to run after the distribution without hurting its real-time constraints. For feasibility analysis and the verification of real-time properties, we had used the schedulability analysis tool SymTA/S [16] in the past. While our prior usage was a model-based offline one, we needed to create a way for an online integration of the schedulability analysis to make it usable by the selfmanager at runtime. This way, the self-manager verifies distribution patterns before actually migrating components.

div.head: Integrating the SymTA/S analysis
div.p: A schedulability analysis by SymTA/S requires a configuration description of the system to be analyzed containing all relevant parameters. A system configuration has to be provided as a model for SymTA/S and contains resources, tasks, channels and event streams (see Fig. 3). A resource can be a processor or a bus. Tasks are assigned to processors while channels are assigned to buses. Functional dependencies are modeled by event streams.

The properties of all model elements can be set individually. Tasks are described by properties like the core time or a priority. Properties of a processor are, for instance, the scheduling algorithm or the time required for a context switch. A typical bus property is the used scheduling algorithm, and channels have properties like the packet size.

The schedulability analysis checks whether the configuration of the system is schedulable or not and has to calculate the worst case response times of all tasks. SymTA/S analyzes the utilization of all resources and examines whether all tasks are executed or maybe are prevented from execution by higher priority tasks. If tasks have deadlines, the analysis also examines whether those deadlines are met. Therefore, SymTA/S calculates and observes possible execution paths and checks if a task chain is executed sufficiently fast. Elements in a chain are connected by event streams and are called a path. The whole configuration is stored in an XML file. Which paths are to be observed and what constraints are to be kept on them can also be defined in that file to exclude impossible execution paths.

For the execution of SymTA/S, we connect an additional PC to our system (see Fig. 1). The selfmanager of the control core reads the system configuration out of the XML file when the system starts and stores it in its knowledge base. When the self-manager decides to evaluate a possible distribution, it manipulates the XML representation of the configuration in memory, transfers it to the analysis PC via a TCP connection and thus triggers the schedulability analysis. SymTA/S is started by a wrapper tool using the Jython script language which also transfers the analysis results back to the control PC. There it becomes part of the self-manager's knowledge base and the self-manager can found decisions about component migration on it.

To make an analysis of our system with SymTA/S possible, we had to create a bus plug-in for the FireWire bus. Since the analysis approach of SymTA/S is based on worst case execution times (WCETs), we had to create algorithms that deliver those WCETs. Using an extension of a busy window technique by Lehoczky [17], we created different algorithms for isochronous and asynchronous FireWire communication.

The accuracy of the analysis can be improved online as measured execution times become available. By monitoring, for instance, time consumption of the FireWire driver for isochronous or asynchronous data transfers, the self-manager can improve the model of the system configuration before he triggers the analysis by SymTA/S. Those time amounts depend on the Node ID assigned during the FireWire root contention protocol and can change for instance when a new component is connected to the bus. An online surveillance of that parameters and a constant refinement of SymTA/S model can thus greatly improve the accuracy of the schedulability analysis.

At the moment, we have to create SymTA/S models of our system prior to an execution. Although those models get adapted later at runtime, the initial model creation task requires a lot of expert knowledge about the underlying bus architecture and the system components. There is research going on in the field of automatic model generation where all execution times, communication between components and other relevant system parameters are observed and then used to create SymTA/S models automatically during system execution [18]. This promising organic approach will greatly ease the online application of SymTA/S for schedulability analysis.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We have presented a software architecture for parallel kinematic machines and our plans to integrate self-managers to encapsulate expert knowledge and create a self-adaptive system. We introduced our tool based, simulation supported development approach and described a first realization of a self-manager for the control core that uses schedulability analysis to verify its real-time properties prior to adapting the system to a new situation. Plans to provide further formal methods to support decisions by the self-managers were outlined.
